title: Conversational throughput tiering and adaptive streaming minimums research
creator: Aisha Mendes
description:
Objective: evaluate a conversational-aware pricing experiment that combines throughput-tiered per-token rates with an adaptive per-connection streaming minimum (grace credits) to reduce churn for low-volume streaming customers while protecting unit economics.

Hypotheses:
1) A small, adaptive streaming minimum (dynamic grace credits based on historical session distribution) will reduce billing surprises for conversational apps that use long-lived streams without materially increasing cost per useful token.
2) Weighting ingress/egress asymmetrically by conversational turn (e.g., system+prompt tokens vs model output tokens) better aligns price with value for chat-first apps and reduces customer objections during SQ/contract review.
3) Usage-tiered per-token rates based on 95th-percentile sustained throughput (tokens/sec) allows predictable pricing for high-throughput customers while preserving revenue from bursty workloads.

Success metrics:
- Revenue delta vs baseline (30d window) and projected 90d impact
- Percentage of streaming sessions charged only at floor vs above floor
- Net churn / cancellation rate for customers using streaming chat SDKs
- Unit cost (GPU token cost) vs realized price by segment
- Legal/SQ friction signals (incidents where enterprise legal requests pricing edits)

Experiment design:
- Two-arm randomized trial across newly onboarded Hosted API customers and opt-in existing customers with streaming traffic. Control = current symmetric per-token pricing with fixed streaming floor. Variant A = throughput-tiered per-token pricing + adaptive streaming grace. Variant B = asymmetric IO weighting + throughput tiers (reserved for enterprise pilot).
- Sampling: stratified by customer size (free, small, mid, enterprise) and predominant workload (chat, completion, embedding).
- Duration: rolling 90-day window with 14d minimum for early signal evaluation. Rollback criteria: >10% negative revenue swing after adjusting for seasonality or >3x increase in SQ/legal escalations.

Implementation notes / required changes:
- Billing engine: support dynamic per-connection grace credits and per-request flags for streaming handshake metadata. (ENG-2245)
- Telemetry: new metrics in the hosted-metering pipeline: session_length_tokens, session_duration_ms, stream_active_count, per-request billed_amount, floor_applied boolean. Grafana dashboard for daily cohort view. (ENG-3418)
- SDK/Docs: add streaming-tags and opt-in flags; update quickstart and billing FAQ. (Docs PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/docs/pull/1721)
- Console: add experiment cohort view and per-customer floor exposure in Console billing UI (release target hosted-pricing-2026.04).
- Contract/SQ: map experiment parameters to enterprise SQ language; prepare standard clause and examples for sales to use during negotiation. Link to SQ mapping: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1a2B_experiment_SQ_map

Notes on trade-offs discussed in kickoff:
- Trade-off A: Simplicity vs fairness — flat streaming floors are simpler for invoices but penalize many chat apps that keep long-lived streams for UX. Adaptive grace is more complex to implement but reduces churn risk.
- Trade-off B: Revenue predictability vs customer friendliness — throughput tiers stabilize revenue for high-volume customers but require careful threshold placement to avoid step-charging. We plan to use 95th-percentile throughput smoothing to reduce cliff effects.
- Trade-off C: SQ surface area — asymmetric IO wording introduces more complexity in contracts and may trigger additional compliance review; decided to keep a standard example appendix in the SQ pack to reduce back-and-forth.

- Explore automated grace credit tuning using historical session percentiles per-customer.
- Consider offering a "streaming-friendly" small monthly bundle for low-volume chat apps as an alternative to floors.
